name: research_critique
held_out: Each case was written from a named flaw in the philosophy-of-science literature (ad hoc immunisation, circularity, ignoring disconfirming evidence, generalising from a single case), not from reading olivia/research/critic.py's checks. No case was edited or removed after scores were seen, and no marker phrase from the solver's _UNFALSIFIABLE_MARKERS list was planted deliberately.
fairness_rule: Every flawed case is structurally clean apart from its single target flaw: each experiment declares a controlled variable, has sample_size >= 10, and is analysed; every analysis reporting a p-value also reports an effect size. So a catch on a semantic family is a catch on the epistemics, not an accidental hit on a structural rule. The two *_structural families are the deliberate exception — they exist to confirm the structural rules still fire.

families.unfalsifiable_structural: Hypothesis missing its predictions or its refutation test — the form the symbolic checker was built to catch.
families.unfalsifiable_semantic: All fields present and plausible-looking, but the content cannot be refuted by any observation.
families.circular: The prediction or the refutation test restates the hypothesis; the explanation is true by construction.
families.contradicted_by_evidence: The cycle's own analysis disconfirms the hypothesis, which is nonetheless carried forward as supported.
families.overfit_n1_structural: Experiment declares a sample size below the underpowered threshold.
families.overfit_n1_semantic: A universal claim rests on an analysis of a single case, while the plan on paper claims a full sample.
families.sound: Control cases: falsifiable, controlled, powered, analysed, and honestly interpreted. Flagging these is a false alarm.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: No predictions and no refutation test.
cases.question: What drives long-term learning outcomes?

hypotheses.statement: Motivation is the primary driver of long-term learning outcomes.
hypotheses.rationale: Motivated learners persist longer.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-sample t-test with Hedges' g.

analyses.summary: Framed group scored higher at 8 weeks.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Predictions present but no refutation test.
cases.question: How does sleep affect memory consolidation?

hypotheses.statement: Slow-wave sleep in the first half of the night consolidates declarative memory.
hypotheses.rationale: Consolidation is thought to depend on hippocampal replay during slow-wave sleep.
predictions: Recall of word pairs is higher after a night with intact slow-wave sleep than after selective slow-wave deprivation.

experiments.analysis_plan: Paired t-test with Cohen's dz.

analyses.summary: Recall dropped after selective deprivation.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Refutation test present but no predictions.
cases.question: Does interleaving improve transfer?

hypotheses.statement: Interleaved practice improves transfer to novel problems relative to blocked practice.
hypotheses.rationale: Interleaving forces discrimination between problem types.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Randomise learners to interleaved or blocked practice; equal transfer scores refute the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: ANCOVA on transfer score with pretest as covariate.

analyses.summary: Interleaved group transferred better.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Ad hoc immunisation: any failure is reattributed to misidentification of the style, so no result can count against it.
cases.question: Should instruction be matched to a learner's cognitive style?

hypotheses.statement: Every learner has a latent cognitive style that fixes the optimal mode of instruction; where matched instruction fails to help, the learner's style was misidentified.
hypotheses.rationale: Style-matched instruction is widely reported to help when the match is correct.
predictions: Instruction matched to a correctly identified style outperforms mismatched instruction.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Re-identify the learner's true style and repeat the matched instruction; persistent failure indicates the style was still mislabelled.

experiments.analysis_plan: Mixed-effects model with style as a moderator.

analyses.summary: No style-by-mode interaction; cases of no benefit were reclassified as mislabelled styles.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The posited entity has no independent trace: the only evidence for the field is the outcome it is invoked to explain.
cases.question: Why do some study groups outperform others?

hypotheses.statement: A field of collective attention modulates group study performance; the field leaves no trace apart from the performance it produces.
hypotheses.rationale: Groups sometimes outperform the sum of their members.
predictions: Groups under a stronger collective-attention field score higher on the group task.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Compare the performance of groups with a strong field against groups with a weak field.

experiments.analysis_plan: Correlate inferred field strength with task score.

analyses.summary: Inferred field strength correlates with task score, as it must by construction.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The key term is defined by the outcome: 'truly learned' just means 'retained', so no forgetting can ever count against it.
cases.question: Is forgetting evidence of incomplete learning?

hypotheses.statement: Anything a student forgets was never truly learned, since true learning is permanent by its nature.
hypotheses.rationale: Durable knowledge is the mark of genuine understanding.
predictions: No item that was truly learned is ever found to be forgotten at a later test.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Identify an item a student truly learned and later forgot.

experiments.analysis_plan: Compare retention across mastery classes.

analyses.summary: Forgotten items were reclassified after the fact as never mastered.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Every possible outcome confirms it: any schedule that helps is evidence, and individual variation absorbs every schedule that does not.
cases.question: Why does spaced repetition work?

hypotheses.statement: Spaced repetition works because memory is attuned to an inner rhythm that expresses itself differently in each person, so whichever schedule helps a given learner reveals that learner's rhythm.
hypotheses.rationale: Optimal spacing intervals differ between individuals.
predictions: For every learner there exists some spacing schedule that outperforms massed practice.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Find a learner for whom no spacing schedule whatsoever beats massed practice.

experiments.analysis_plan: Per-learner best-schedule comparison against massed practice.

analyses.summary: The best-performing schedule per learner beat massed practice, by selection.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: 'Effective study' is operationalised as 'study that yields better grades', so the hypothesis states an identity.
cases.question: Does effective study improve grades?

hypotheses.statement: Students who study effectively obtain better grades, because effective study is precisely the study that produces better grades.
hypotheses.rationale: Effectiveness is measured by the grades achieved.
predictions: Students classified as effective studiers obtain better grades than those classified as ineffective.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Find a student classified as an effective studier whose grades are poor.

experiments.analysis_plan: Compare mean grades across effectiveness classes.

analyses.summary: Effective studiers had higher grades, as the classification guarantees.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Dormitive-virtue explanation: the cause is named after the effect it is supposed to explain.
cases.question: Why does compound A induce sleep?

hypotheses.statement: Compound A induces sleep because it possesses a soporific property, that property being its capacity to induce sleep.
hypotheses.rationale: Subjects given compound A fall asleep sooner.
predictions: Subjects given compound A fall asleep sooner than subjects given placebo.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Administer compound A and observe no reduction in sleep latency.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-sample comparison of sleep latency.

analyses.summary: Sleep latency fell in the compound A arm.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The independent variable is identified by the dependent variable, so the prediction cannot fail.
cases.question: What makes a school high performing?

hypotheses.statement: High-performing schools perform highly because they possess a culture of excellence, and a culture of excellence is identified by the school's high performance.
hypotheses.rationale: Site visits to top schools consistently report a culture of excellence.
predictions: Schools identified as having a culture of excellence outperform schools that lack one.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Find a school with a culture of excellence whose performance is low.

experiments.analysis_plan: Regress performance index on culture rating.

analyses.summary: Culture rating predicts performance almost perfectly, as the rating is derived from it.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The refutation test is stated in terms that the hypothesis's own definitions make impossible to satisfy.
cases.question: Do adaptive learning systems personalise instruction?

hypotheses.statement: An adaptive system personalises instruction, where personalised instruction means whatever an adaptive system delivers.
hypotheses.rationale: Adaptive systems adjust content per learner.
predictions: Instruction delivered by an adaptive system is personalised.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Observe an adaptive system delivering instruction that is not personalised.

experiments.analysis_plan: Compare personalisation index across arms.

analyses.summary: Adaptive arm scored higher on the personalisation index, which is computed from adaptivity.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: A null result with a tight interval is carried forward as support; the hypothesis is marked supported at 0.85 confidence.
cases.question: Do blue-light filters before bed improve next-day recall?

hypotheses.statement: Wearing blue-light filtering glasses for two hours before bed improves next-day recall of studied material.
hypotheses.rationale: Blue light suppresses melatonin, which may impair consolidation.
predictions: Filter nights are followed by higher morning recall than control nights.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A crossover trial in which filter and control nights yield equal recall refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Paired comparison with Cohen's dz and a 95% CI.

analyses.summary: No detectable difference between filter and control nights.
analyses.interpretation: The interval excludes any effect of practical size.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The measured effect runs opposite to the prediction and is significant, yet the hypothesis is retained at 0.9 confidence.
cases.question: Does a pre-study mindfulness session raise quiz scores?

hypotheses.statement: A ten-minute mindfulness session immediately before studying raises quiz scores.
hypotheses.rationale: Reduced mind-wandering should improve encoding.
predictions: The mindfulness arm scores higher on the post-study quiz than the control arm.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A randomised trial in which the mindfulness arm scores no higher refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-sample t-test with Hedges' g.

analyses.summary: The mindfulness arm scored lower than control.
analyses.interpretation: The effect is significant and in the opposite direction to the prediction.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: A null result is reported and the hypothesis is nonetheless left standing as supported.
cases.question: Do handwritten notes beat typed notes for conceptual recall?

hypotheses.statement: Taking notes by hand produces better conceptual recall than typing them.
hypotheses.rationale: Handwriting is slower and may force generative processing.
predictions: The handwriting arm scores higher on conceptual items one week later.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A randomised trial in which the two arms score equally on conceptual items refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: ANCOVA with prior-knowledge covariate.

analyses.summary: Conceptual recall did not differ by medium.
analyses.interpretation: No support for a medium effect at this sample size.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: Disconfirming evidence is present in evidence_against and ignored in the hypothesis's status and confidence.
cases.question: Does background music raise reading comprehension?

hypotheses.statement: Instrumental background music raises reading comprehension.
hypotheses.rationale: Music is reported to raise arousal during study.
predictions: Comprehension scores are higher with background music than in silence.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A within-subject trial in which silence yields equal or better comprehension refutes the hypothesis.
evidence_against: Our own trial found comprehension lower with music (g = -0.42, p = 0.001).

experiments.analysis_plan: Paired comparison with Hedges' g.

analyses.summary: Comprehension was lower with music than in silence.
analyses.interpretation: The evidence points the other way.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The experiment declares a sample size of 1.
cases.question: Does a ketogenic diet raise exam performance in adolescents?

hypotheses.statement: A ketogenic diet raises exam performance in adolescents.
hypotheses.rationale: One student's marks rose after starting the diet.
predictions: Adolescents on the diet score higher on end-of-term exams than matched controls.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A controlled trial in which diet and control groups score equally refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Compare exam scores across phases.

analyses.summary: The participant's scores rose during the diet phase.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: The experiment declares a sample size of 3.
cases.question: Does a standing desk improve sustained attention?

hypotheses.statement: Working at a standing desk improves sustained attention during study.
hypotheses.rationale: Postural change may raise arousal.
predictions: Sustained-attention task scores are higher at a standing desk than seated.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A crossover trial in which the two conditions score equally refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Paired comparison across conditions.

analyses.summary: Two of three participants scored higher standing.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: A universal claim rests on an analysis of one participant, while the plan on paper claims a sample of 40.
cases.question: Does a morning cold shower improve learning?

hypotheses.statement: A morning cold shower improves learning for everyone who takes one.
hypotheses.rationale: A single volunteer reported sharper focus and better recall after adopting the habit.
predictions: Recall scores rise on cold-shower mornings relative to warm-shower mornings.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A crossover trial in which recall does not differ by shower temperature refutes the hypothesis.
evidence_for: One volunteer's self-reported improvement over three weeks.

experiments.analysis_plan: Paired comparison across conditions.

analyses.summary: Only one participant completed the protocol; that participant's recall rose 18%, and the result is reported as if it were the group finding.

cases.label: flawed
cases.flaw: A single classroom's result is generalised to every subject and every age group.
cases.question: Does a flipped classroom raise achievement?

hypotheses.statement: The flipped-classroom format raises achievement in every subject and at every age.
hypotheses.rationale: One flipped Year 10 physics class outperformed its previous cohort.
predictions: Flipped classes outscore conventional classes on end-of-unit assessments.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A trial in which flipped and conventional classes score equally refutes the hypothesis.
evidence_for: One Year 10 physics class, one term.

experiments.analysis_plan: Compare assessment means between cohorts.

analyses.summary: The single flipped class outscored its comparison cohort; the conclusion is stated for all subjects and ages.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does retrieval practice beat rereading for long-term retention?

hypotheses.statement: Retrieval practice produces higher retention at one week than an equal amount of rereading.
hypotheses.rationale: Retrieval is thought to strengthen the memory trace more than restudy.
predictions: The retrieval arm scores higher on a one-week delayed test.
The advantage grows with retention interval.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A randomised trial with matched study time in which retrieval scores no higher at one week refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-sample t-test with Hedges' g and a 95% CI.

analyses.summary: Retrieval practice outperformed rereading at one week.
analyses.interpretation: A moderate effect with an interval excluding zero.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does spacing beat massing at a fixed total study time?

hypotheses.statement: Distributing study across three sessions produces higher two-week retention than one massed session of the same total length.
hypotheses.rationale: The spacing effect is among the most replicated findings in memory research.
predictions: The spaced arm scores higher at two weeks.
Immediate post-test scores do not differ, or favour massing.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A trial with equal total study time in which the spaced arm scores no higher at two weeks refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: ANCOVA with pretest covariate; report g and CI.

analyses.summary: Spaced study retained more at two weeks.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does worked-example study beat problem solving for novices?

hypotheses.statement: For learners without prior algebra knowledge, studying worked examples yields higher post-test scores than solving equivalent problems unaided.
hypotheses.rationale: Cognitive-load theory predicts an advantage for novices.
predictions: Novices in the worked-example arm score higher on the post-test.
The advantage shrinks or reverses for learners with prior knowledge.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A trial in which novices in both arms score equally refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Stratified analysis reporting g and CI per stratum.

analyses.summary: Novices gained from worked examples; the effect reversed for the high-prior-knowledge stratum.
analyses.interpretation: Supports the hypothesis, including its boundary condition.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does sleep after study beat an equal waking interval for retention?

hypotheses.statement: A twelve-hour interval containing sleep produces higher retention than a twelve-hour waking interval.
hypotheses.rationale: Consolidation is thought to be favoured by sleep.
predictions: The sleep-interval group recalls more at test.
The difference is larger for declarative than for procedural material.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Equal recall across the two intervals, with time of day counterbalanced, refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-way ANOVA; report partial eta squared and CIs.

analyses.summary: Recall was higher across the sleep interval.
analyses.interpretation: Moderate effect, time of day counterbalanced.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does self-explanation improve transfer in physics problem solving?

hypotheses.statement: Prompting learners to self-explain each solution step raises transfer-problem scores relative to unprompted study.
hypotheses.rationale: Self-explanation is thought to surface gaps in the learner's model.
predictions: The prompted arm scores higher on transfer problems.
Near-transfer and far-transfer gains differ in size.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Equal transfer scores between prompted and unprompted arms refute the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Report g with 95% CI for near and far transfer separately.

analyses.summary: Near transfer improved; far transfer showed a smaller, uncertain gain.
analyses.interpretation: Partial support; far transfer remains open.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does handwriting speed predict essay quality once vocabulary is controlled?

hypotheses.statement: Handwriting speed does not predict essay quality once vocabulary breadth is controlled.
hypotheses.rationale: Earlier correlations may be confounded by vocabulary.
predictions: The partial correlation between handwriting speed and essay quality is near zero.
The zero-order correlation is positive.
hypotheses.falsification_test: A substantial partial correlation after controlling vocabulary refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Partial correlation with bootstrap CI.

analyses.summary: The partial correlation was near zero once vocabulary was controlled.
analyses.interpretation: Consistent with the null hypothesis as stated.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does immediate feedback beat delayed feedback on procedural skills?

hypotheses.statement: Immediate feedback produces faster skill acquisition but no better one-week retention than delayed feedback.
hypotheses.rationale: Immediate feedback may support performance during practice without aiding consolidation.
predictions: Acquisition curves are steeper under immediate feedback.
One-week retention does not differ between conditions.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Higher one-week retention under immediate feedback refutes the second half of the hypothesis.

experiments.design: randomised controlled with delayed retention test
experiments.analysis_plan: Mixed model over trials; report g and CI at retention.

analyses.summary: Acquisition was faster with immediate feedback; retention did not differ.
analyses.interpretation: Both halves of the prediction held.

cases.label: sound
cases.question: Does a pre-lecture quiz improve lecture recall?

hypotheses.statement: A short quiz taken before a lecture raises recall of lecture content measured one day later.
hypotheses.rationale: Pretesting is reported to direct attention during subsequent study.
predictions: The pre-quiz arm recalls more one day later.
The gain is concentrated on content the pre-quiz touched.
hypotheses.falsification_test: Equal next-day recall between pre-quiz and control arms refutes the hypothesis.

experiments.analysis_plan: Two-sample comparison split by pre-quizzed and non-pre-quizzed content.

analyses.summary: Next-day recall was higher, concentrated on pre-quizzed content.
